rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no baseline performance to reference. The most critical uncertainty is the performance floor of the simplest RNA-only model, which will calibrate whether more complex design choices (learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, multimodal fusion) actually add value. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space—a standard PCA reduction with no learned encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. It establishes the baseline accuracy/F1 for RNA-based classification under the most minimal pipeline. 3) Why it is the best use of the first experiment: Starting with the simplest baseline is the highest-information first step because it anchors all subsequent comparisons. Every later experiment (multiprofile, scvi/scgpt encoders, image-only, multimodal) will be interpreted relative to this floor. Without it, we cannot tell whether a 2-3% gain from a complex multimodal model is meaningful or just noise. It also avoids the risk of over-investing in a complex configuration before knowing whether the simpler signal is already sufficient.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), the most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any useful signal for this task. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_001: it holds profile setting (singleprofile) and structural simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion) constant while switching modality from RNA to image. If image accuracy is substantially higher, it justifies investing further experiments in multimodal fusion and ViT encoders; if it is comparable or lower, it suggests RNA is the primary signal and the search should focus on RNA encoder and profile/aggregation choices. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality) before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) only reaches 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. With only two data points, the largest uncertainty is whether a learned RNA representation can substantially improve over the PCA baseline. Question: config_007 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001—only the RNA encoder changes. scgpt is a pretrained generative model for single-cell data that may capture richer biological structure than linear PCA. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It isolates the effect of representation quality on the dominant modality without confounding with profile, aggregation, or fusion changes. (2) The outcome directly guides all subsequent experiments—if scgpt substantially improves, we exploit that encoder across profile/fusion settings; if it does not, PCA is competitive and we pivot to testing multiprofile/aggregation or multimodal fusion. (3) Under a limited budget, resolving whether learned representations matter for the primary signal source is the highest-information single experiment available.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the best result so far at 0.485 acc, while scgpt (config_007, 0.411) underperforms and image-only resnet50 (config_010, 0.208) is very weak. The profile setting (single vs multi) is a critical, untested design axis that affects a large portion of the configuration space. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve upon the best singleprofile RNA result, while keeping the proven pca_n2000 encoder fixed? Why this is best: config_002 is a minimal, controlled change from config_001 (only profile setting and aggregation change), isolating the effect of multiprofile. Starting with avgpool (simpler aggregation) before transformer avoids confounding two new variables. The outcome directly informs whether to invest further experiments in multiprofile + transformer, multimodal multiprofile, or to abandon multiprofile altogether—making it the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA_n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, showing a large ~10.6% gain over single-profile PCA (config_001, 0.485). This strongly suggests multi-profile aggregation is a key design lever. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple avgpool in the multi-profile setting, or whether avgpool already captures most of the benefit. This experiment (config_003) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model setting, profile setting, and encoder fixed to the best-known combination, giving a clean single-variable comparison. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends the strongest evidence, isolates the aggregation effect, and the result will inform all subsequent multi-profile and multimodal experiments (configs 020, 021, 026, 027, etc.) where aggregation choice is a critical design decision.

Evidence: Multi-profile + avgpool with PCA (config_002, acc=0.591) is the strongest result so far, a clear ~10-point gain over single-profile PCA (0.485), and avgpool beats transformer (0.519). However, scVI is completely untested across all experiments, leaving a major gap in encoder knowledge. This experiment (RNA-only, multi-profile, scVI, avgpool) isolates the encoder variable by swapping PCA→scVI while holding the best-known profile and aggregation settings fixed. It will clarify whether a learned variational encoder can match or exceed the simple PCA baseline in the strongest RNA configuration. This is the best next step because it reduces uncertainty about a critical, unexplored design axis with a clean single-variable comparison before investing budget in more complex multimodal experiments where encoder choice would be confounded with fusion effects.

The current best result is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. We have evidence that avgpool outperformed transformer for pca_n2000 (0.591 vs 0.519), but it is unclear whether this aggregation preference holds for the stronger scvi_n200 encoder, whose learned latent representations may interact differently with attention-based pooling. Config_006 is a clean single-variable comparison (only aggregation changes) against the current best, isolating the aggregation effect for scvi_n200. If avgpool wins again, we can confidently lock in avgpool for all future multimodal experiments and pivot to testing fusion strategies; if transformer wins, we learn that scvi_n200's structured latent space benefits from attention, which would change our aggregation choice for every downstream configuration. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile achieves ~0.65 acc (configs 005/006), far exceeding pca_n2000 singleprofile (0.485) and scgpt singleprofile (0.411). For pca_n2000, multiprofile+avgpool gave a ~0.106 boost over singleprofile, but we have no data on whether scvi_n200 benefits similarly from multiprofile or is already strong in singleprofile. Question: config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) isolates the profile-setting effect for the best-performing RNA encoder with only one variable changed relative to configs 005/006. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean single-factor comparison that directly tests whether the multiprofile gain is encoder-dependent or universal. (2) The result determines whether future multimodal experiments should use multiprofile or singleprofile for scvi_n200, saving budget by avoiding redundant variants. (3) It is lower-risk and more interpretable than jumping to a multimodal config where multiple new factors (image encoder, fusion strategy) would confound the result. (4) If scvi_n200 singleprofile is already competitive (~0.60+), it shifts focus toward fusion/image questions; if it drops substantially, it confirms multiprofile is essential and narrows the search space.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the clear best pipeline (acc ~0.65), while image-only with resnet50 is very weak (acc 0.208). The critical open question is whether adding image features to the best RNA pipeline provides any benefit, or whether image is simply uninformative for this task. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) takes the best RNA configuration and adds the simplest possible image contribution (concat fusion with resnet50). It tests one focused question: does image add signal on top of scvi_n200 multiprofile RNA? If performance drops or stays flat, we can eliminate the large multimodal search space and focus budget on refining the RNA pipeline. If it improves, we confirm a multimodal direction and know where to invest next. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice because it gates ~30+ downstream configurations, and it changes only the minimal set of variables (adding image + concat) relative to the proven best RNA-only setup.

Evidence: The best RNA-only model (config_005/006, scvi_n200 multiprofile) achieves ~0.650-0.653 accuracy, while the only multimodal experiment (config_030, scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) scores 0.632 — actually below the RNA-only baseline. This suggests concat fusion may be diluting the strong RNA signal with weak image features (resnet50 alone is only 0.208). Question: Does switching from concat to weighted fusion allow the model to down-weight the weak image branch and recover or exceed the RNA-only performance? Why this experiment: config_031 changes exactly one variable (fusion: concat→weighted) relative to config_030, isolating the fusion mechanism. If weighted fusion recovers to ≥0.650, it confirms the image carries marginal signal that needs proper weighting; if it remains below 0.650, we gain strong evidence that resnet50 image features are unhelpful and should pivot to ViT-L (config_036/037). This is the most budget-efficient next step because it directly resolves whether the current multimodal setup is salvageable before committing experiments to a different image encoder.
